newsitem.title: UK: U.K. commodity trade faces higher regulatory costs.
newsitem.headline: U.K. commodity trade faces higher regulatory costs.

text.p: British commodity trading companies face the prospect of sharply higher costs if latest European Commission proposals on financial market regulations are adopted.

On Tuesday, the Commission proposed that the European Union (EU) legislate an amended Capital Adequacy Directive (CAD) which allows banks to use internal models to calculate the capital needed to cover risk.
Commodity companies would have a transition period up to 1999 to adopt this, although there is some uncertainty over which firms come under the proposal, commodity sources said.
"As far as I can see, this will not affect us, but I have not seen the proposals in detail," a director at one major commodity trader said.
"It is going to cost firms whatever they do...and it is a bad time to be piling on regulatory costs," Anthony Belchambers, executive-director of the Futures and Options Association (FOA) said.

Officials at the U.K. major commodity markets the London International Financial Futures Exchange (LIFFE), the London Metal Exchange (LME), and the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) were not immediately available to comment.

Despite lobbying by U.K. finance authorities and agencies such as the Securities and Futures Association (SFA) and FOA, it appears certain a uniform capital requirement will be applied to those firms that are deemed to carry out ISD business (Investment Services Directive).

"We have firmly and consistently argued that the CAD2 (Capital Adequacy Directive) proposals on a single capital requirement are not appropriate for commodities which display very different volatilities and for which a grading approach would be more suitable," the SFA said.
For banks, who do ISD business, commodities make up a relatively small part of their activities, so the capital requirements using a uniform VaR (value-at-risk) model are not great.
But the commodity component of the capital requirement model is based on a highly volatile oil product, which is unsuitable for many commodity companies, sources said.
The new ruling will only apply to those commodity companies covered by the ISD, while capital requirements for non-ISD commodity firms are likely to be at the discretion of the SFA.
ISD commodity companies may be faced with re-locating or parent companies making their subsidiaries non-ISD.
Whatever transpires, Europe's commodity traders, most of which are based in the U.K., will be facing steeper regulatory costs.
"Companies will have to have more capital to do business, which could be excessive," Belchambers said.
Although the Commission proposals have still to be approved by the EU Council and Parliament, there appears to be little doubt they will be passed.
The U.K. did table an alternative approach, which recognised that the range of commodities exhibit very different volatilities.
But the U.K. received very little support from other EU member states, largely for political reasons, regulatory sources said.
